d: The second most common type of breast cancer. It grows diffusely, is harder to see on mammograms and behaves in its own way.
n: At a glance How common 10-15% of invasive breast cancers Who Women slightly older than average; linked to hormone replacement therapy Feature Cells lose the protein E-cadherin and grow loosely, in single files Diagnosis Can be missed on mammography; MRI helps measure it Biology Almost always hormone receptor-positive and HER2-negative What it is Invasive lobular carcinoma starts in the cells of the lobules, the glands that make milk. n: At a glance How common About 1% of all breast cancers Age Mostly between 60 and 70 Typical sign A painless lump behind the nipple Inheritance 10-15% have an inherited variant, mainly in BRCA2 Biology Over 90% hormone receptor-positive What it is Men also have a small amount of breast tissue behind the nipple, where cancer can develop. It is almost always invasive carcinoma of no special type that is oestrogen receptor-positive . d: One of the few cancers that can be almost completely prevented, with HPV vaccination and screening. Causes, precancer, symptoms, treatment and outlook.
n: At a glance How common About 660,000 cases and 350,000 deaths a year worldwide Cause Persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV) Prevention HPV vaccination and screening with HPV testing or cytology Symptoms Bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause; abnormal discharge Treatment Surgery in early stages; chemoradiotherapy with brachytherapy for locally advanced disease Survival About 65-70% at five years; over 90% in early stages What it is The cervix is the lower part of the womb that opens into the vagina. d: The most common gynaecological cancer in high-income countries. It usually warns early with bleeding after menopause, and most are found at an early stage, when surgery is often enough. Molecular classification now guides treatment.
n: At a glance How common About 420,000 cases a year worldwide Who Mostly women over 55, after menopause Typical sign Any vaginal bleeding after menopause Risk factors Obesity, excess oestrogen, diabetes, Lynch syndrome, tamoxifen Treatment Hysterectomy with tubes and ovaries; radiotherapy, chemotherapy and immunotherapy depending on risk Survival About 75-80% at five years; over 90% at stage I What it is The endometrium is the lining of the womb that renews with each period. d: Uncommon malignant tumours arising in the muscle or supporting tissue of the womb. They are often mistaken for fibroids.
n: At a glance How common 3-7% of uterine cancers Types Leiomyosarcoma, low- and high-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma, adenosarcoma Symptoms Abnormal bleeding, pain, a womb that grows quickly Difficulty It is hard to tell from a fibroid before surgery Treatment Complete hysterectomy without fragmenting the womb What it is Uterine sarcomas arise in the myometrium (the muscle of the womb) or the endometrial stroma . d: An uncommon cancer of the external female genitals. Persistent itching or a sore that does not heal should be checked; there are two pathways, one linked to HPV and one to lichen sclerosus.

n: At a glance How common 1-2% of gynaecological cancers; about 18,000 cases a year worldwide Who Mostly women over 60 Main cause Persistent HPV infection Symptoms Bleeding after sex or after menopause, discharge, lump Treatment External radiotherapy and brachytherapy, with cisplatin; surgery in selected cases What it is Primary vaginal cancer is very rare: most tumours found in the vagina come from other organs (cervix, endometrium, vulva, rectum). d: The cancer that causes the most deaths worldwide. Tobacco causes most cases. Low-dose CT screening in smokers, and targeted therapy and immunotherapy in selected tumours, have improved the outlook for some patients.
n: At a glance How common 2.5 million cases a year worldwide (the most common) Deaths 1.8 million a year: almost one in five cancer deaths Main cause Tobacco (80-85%); also radon, asbestos, air pollution Types Non-small cell (85%): adenocarcinoma, squamous; small cell (15%) Detection Yearly low-dose CT screening in high-risk people Treatment Surgery, stereotactic radiotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy Survival Over 60-80% at stage I; about 20-25% at five years overall What it is Lung cancer starts in the cells lining the bronchi and alveoli . d: The most aggressive type of lung cancer, almost always in smokers. It grows and spreads quickly but responds at first to chemotherapy; immunotherapy and tarlatamab have opened new options.
n: At a glance How common 13-15% of lung cancers Cause Tobacco in over 95% Behaviour Grows very fast and spreads early (brain, liver, bone) Stages Limited (one side of the chest) or extensive (two in three at diagnosis) Treatment Chemoradiotherapy for limited; chemo-immunotherapy for extensive What it is Small cell lung cancer ("oat cell") is a high-grade neuroendocrine tumour. Its cells divide very quickly, so the disease has usually spread by diagnosis. It almost always loses the tumour suppressor genes TP53 and RB1 . They belong to a family whose aggressive end includes large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma and small cell cancer . Typical carcinoid : fewer than 2 mitoses per field and no necrosis; rarely spreads. d: Rare tumours of the thymus, a gland behind the breastbone. They are linked to autoimmune diseases such as myasthenia gravis.
n: At a glance How common Very rare: 1-3 cases per million people a year Who Adults aged 40-60 Association Myasthenia gravis in a third of thymomas Treatment Complete surgery (thymectomy); radiotherapy and chemotherapy as needed What they are The thymus is an organ in the front of the chest that helps T lymphocytes mature in childhood and then shrinks. d: A cancer that has fallen sharply in Europe but remains common worldwide. Helicobacter pylori is its main avoidable cause; in localised tumours, chemotherapy before and after surgery improves the outlook.
n: At a glance Frequency About 970,000 cases a year worldwide (GLOBOCAN 2022) and about 7,000 in Spain Causes Helicobacter pylori , smoking, a diet high in salt and salted foods, obesity (at the junction with the oesophagus), inherited factors in a minority Signs Persistent indigestion, feeling full quickly, weight loss, anaemia, black stools Diagnosis Gastroscopy with biopsy Treatment Endoscopic removal if very early; chemotherapy before and after gastrectomy; chemotherapy with immunotherapy or targeted therapy if advanced What it is Stomach (gastric) cancer starts in the lining of the stomach.

d: An uncommon but very difficult cancer, with two distinct types: squamous cell carcinoma, linked to smoking and alcohol, and adenocarcinoma, linked to reflux and obesity. Difficulty swallowing is its main sign.

n: At a glance How common About 50,000 cases a year worldwide; rising Cause HPV (mainly type 16) in 90% Higher risk People with HIV, men who have sex with men, women with cervical or vulval lesions, transplant recipients, smokers Treatment Chemoradiotherapy (mitomycin and 5-FU or capecitabine) Survival 70-80% at five years; over 85% for small tumours What it is The anal canal is the last 3-4 cm of the digestive tract. n: At a glance How common Under 5% of digestive cancers Types Neuroendocrine tumours (ileum), adenocarcinoma (duodenum), GIST, lymphomas Risk factors Crohn's disease, coeliac disease, Lynch, familial adenomatous polyposis, Peutz-Jeghers Symptoms Colicky pain, obstruction, anaemia, bleeding Treatment Surgery; chemotherapy for advanced adenocarcinoma What it is The small bowel (duodenum, jejunum and ileum) is several metres long, yet its cancers are rare. d: A sarcoma of the digestive tract that marked a milestone: it was the first solid tumour in which a targeted tablet, imatinib, controlled advanced disease for years in many patients with the right mutation.
n: At a glance How common 10-15 cases per million people a year; the most common digestive sarcoma Where Stomach (60%), small bowel (30%), rectum, oesophagus Origin Interstitial cells of Cajal, the bowel's "pacemaker" Key alteration KIT (75-80%) or PDGFRA (10%) mutations Treatment Surgery; imatinib for 3 years if relapse risk is high What it is GIST arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal , described by Santiago Ramón y Cajal, which coordinate bowel movements. d: Tumours arising from hormone-producing cells of the gut. They usually grow slowly and some cause carcinoid syndrome; lutetium-177 has improved their treatment.
n: At a glance How common Rising: about 5-7 cases per 100,000 people a year Where Small bowel (ileum), rectum, appendix, stomach, pancreas, colon Grades G1, G2, G3 by Ki-67 index; neuroendocrine carcinomas are very aggressive Typical symptom Carcinoid syndrome: facial flushing, diarrhoea, sometimes heart valve damage Treatment Surgery; somatostatin analogues, lutetium-177, everolimus, chemotherapy What they are Neuroendocrine cells are scattered throughout the gut and make hormones such as serotonin . d: Rare tumours of the appendix, often found after appendicitis. Some fill the abdomen with mucus (pseudomyxoma) and are treated with surgery and heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy.

d: Tumours of the hormone-making cells of the pancreas. They are much less aggressive than ordinary pancreatic cancer; some produce hormones that cause striking symptoms.

d: Primary liver cancer almost always develops in a liver damaged by hepatitis B or C, alcohol or fat. Ultrasound surveillance of people with cirrhosis allows early detection.

d: Cancer of the bile ducts, inside or outside the liver. It is uncommon and hard to treat, but many carry genetic alterations with targeted treatments.

d: An uncommon cancer in Europe but very common in Chile, Bolivia, India and elsewhere. It is often found by chance after gallbladder removal for stones.

d: The most common cancer in men in Europe. Many grow so slowly that they need no immediate treatment; others are aggressive. PSA, MRI and active surveillance help tell them apart.

d: A comparison of the two main urological cancers after prostate: blood in the urine as a shared sign, smoking as a shared cause, and their treatments. Each organ also has its own main page.
n: This page compares the two cancers. For full information on each, see the main pages: Bladder cancer and Kidney cancer . d: More than half are found by chance on an ultrasound or CT scan. Small tumours are often treated by removing only part of the kidney, and in advanced disease immunotherapy has lengthened survival for many patients.

d: The most common type of kidney cancer. Its biology, linked to the VHL gene and the oxygen-sensing pathway, explains why it responds to anti-angiogenics, immunotherapy and belzutifan.

d: The most common solid cancer in young men and one of the most curable, even with metastases, thanks to cisplatin. Self-examination helps find it early.

d: A rare cancer in Europe but more common in parts of South America, Africa and Asia. It is linked to HPV, phimosis and poor hygiene; caught early it can be treated while preserving the organ.

n: What to expect The first appointment is usually long and full of information. The oncologist will review your history and test results, examine you and explain what is known about the tumour, what is still unknown and what the options are. Often the final plan is not decided that day: more tests are awaited or the case goes to the multidisciplinary team (tumour board), a meeting of surgeons, oncologists, radiation oncologists, pathologists and radiologists who decide together. n: A common topic that is rarely discussed More than half of people treated for cancer notice changes in their sex life. d: What people usually feel when they are diagnosed with cancer, why reactions change over time, what is normal and which signs suggest asking for specialist help.
n: The initial blow Hearing the word "cancer" is one of the hardest moments a person can go through. In the first days it is common to feel: Shock or unreality: "this can't be happening to me". n: Anxiety Anxiety is a constant state of alert: worry that cannot be switched off, restlessness, muscle tension, a racing heart, difficulty breathing or sleeping. It is especially common around tests, results and the start of treatment. Some people have panic attacks or a strong fear of needles, scanners or hospitals. d: Children notice when something is happening at home. How to explain a parent's diagnosis according to their age, what questions they usually ask and which signs show they need help.
n: Why it is worth telling them Children, even very young ones, notice changes: hospital visits, tiredness, crying, whispered conversations. If nobody explains anything, they fill the gaps with their imagination, which is often worse than reality, and may think it is their fault or that they cannot ask. Telling them the truth, adapted to their age, protects their trust and allows them to receive support. How to tell them Choose a calm moment and, if possible, tell them together (both parents, or the parent and a trusted adult). Use the real words: "cancer" , "tumour", " chemotherapy ". Euphemisms

d: Scars, hair loss, a mastectomy or an ostomy change the way people see themselves. How these changes affect self-esteem and relationships, and what helps recovery.
n: The body changes Cancer and its treatments can leave visible and invisible marks: scars , the loss of a breast or part of the body, an ostomy , hair loss, weight changes, skin changes, swelling (lymphoedema), early menopause. Some are temporary and others permanent. It is normal to feel strange in front of the mirror, to avoid looking at yourself or being looked at, or to feel less attractive. These feelings do not depend on how "big" the change is from the outside, but on what it means to each person. They usually ease with time, but sometimes they persist and affect self-esteem, social life

d: A simple explanation: what happens in cells, why it is not a single disease and how it spreads.
n: Cells that lose control The body is made of trillions of cells that divide, do their job and die in an orderly way, following the instructions in their genes. Cancer appears when a cell builds up changes in its DNA that make it divide out of control, ignore signals to stop or die, and escape the body's defences. These changes mainly affect two kinds of genes: oncogenes , which act like a stuck accelerator, and tumour suppressor genes , brakes that stop working. n: Genetic is not the same as inherited Cancer is always a genetic disease, because it arises from changes in cells' DNA. But almost all those changes are acquired during life in a particular cell, and are not passed on to children. Only 5 to 10% of cancers are due to an inherited variant that greatly increases risk, such as those in BRCA1 and BRCA2 or in Lynch syndrome . d: A common fear that delays diagnosis. What studies say about biopsies, surgery and "air" reaching the tumour.
n: The short answer Not in normal practice. The risk of a needle biopsy spreading tumour cells along its track is very low , and doctors take steps to reduce it further, such as planning the needle's path. Delaying or avoiding a biopsy out of fear is dangerous, because without it the type of cancer cannot be known or the right treatment chosen. Studies of thousands of patients, for example in breast or prostate cancer, have not shown that biopsy worsens survival. d: Sugar, mobile phones, deodorants, stress, sweeteners or microwaves. What the evidence says about the most repeated worries.
n: "Sugar feeds cancer" All cells, healthy ones too, use glucose. Eating sugar does not specifically make a tumour grow, and cutting it out completely does not cure it. What does matter is that excess calories lead to obesity , which increases the risk of several cancers. "Mobile phones cause brain cancer" IARC classified them in 2011 as "possibly carcinogenic" (Group 2B) on limited evidence. Later studies, including a review commissioned by the WHO in 2024, have found no increase in brain tumour risk, despite the huge rise in use. d: The number of cases is rising, but the risk of dying from cancer at each age is falling. The reasons are ageing, earlier diagnosis and some habits.

d: Treatment given after the main treatment, usually surgery, to reduce the risk of relapse. It may be chemotherapy, radiotherapy, hormone therapy or immunotherapy.
The formation of new blood vessels. Tumours stimulate it to get oxygen and nutrients, and some drugs block it.
An antibody linked to a very potent drug, which it delivers directly to cells carrying its target. Also called an ADC.
A tumour that does not invade nearby tissue or spread. It can cause problems through its size or location, but it is not a cancer.
A measurable feature that tells us about a tumour: for example a hormone receptor, HER2, a mutation or PD-L1. It helps choose treatment.
Taking a tissue sample to examine under the microscope. It is the test that confirms the diagnosis of most cancers.
Radiotherapy in which the radioactive source is placed inside or very close to the tumour. Used, for example, in cervical or prostate cancer.
Genes that help repair DNA. Inherited variants that inactivate them greatly increase the risk of breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancer.
A treatment in which a patient's T cells are collected, modified in the laboratory to recognise cancer cells and infused back.
An agent that can cause cancer, such as tobacco smoke, asbestos or ultraviolet radiation. IARC classifies them by the strength of the evidence.
Cancer arising from epithelial cells, which line the skin, organs and glands. It is the most common type of cancer.
A lesion with malignant cells that have not yet broken through the layer where they started. It does not spread, but may progress if untreated.
A drug that blocks the immune system's "brakes", such as PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4, so that lymphocytes attack the tumour.
Treatment with drugs that destroy fast-dividing cells. It can cure, reduce the risk of relapse or control the disease.
A study in people comparing a new treatment with the usual treatment to find out whether it is effective and safe. It has phases and eligibility criteria.
The percentage of people in a group still alive five years after diagnosis. It is a statistical measure, not a deadline.
Describes a genetic variant present in every cell of the body from birth. It can be inherited. The opposite of somatic.
A description of how different tumour cells look from normal cells under the microscope. A high grade usually means faster growth.
A protein that, when present in excess in breast or stomach tumour cells, drives their growth. There are specific drugs against it.
Treatment that blocks or reduces the hormones that drive some cancers, mainly breast and prostate cancer.
Human papillomavirus. Some types cause almost all cervical cancers and some anal, penile, vulvar and oropharyngeal cancers. There is a vaccine.
A laboratory technique that stains specific proteins in a tissue sample. It helps identify a tumour's type and which treatments may work.
Treatment that helps the immune system recognise and destroy cancer cells.
Cancer of the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. It can be acute or chronic, and lymphoid or myeloid.
A test of blood or other fluids looking for fragments of tumour DNA or other signs of cancer. It has specific uses, and others still under research.
Cancer of lymphocytes that usually affects the lymph nodes. Divided into Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
An inherited predisposition to colorectal, endometrial and other cancers, caused by variants in DNA repair genes.
A tumour able to invade nearby tissue and spread to other organs. A synonym for cancer.
The time at which half the people in a study are still alive. The other half live longer. It does not predict what will happen to one person.
A tumour formed by cells that have broken away from the original tumour and travelled to another organ in the blood or lymph.
A sign that the tumour cell does not correct DNA copying errors properly. Linked to Lynch syndrome and predicts a good response to immunotherapy.
A laboratory-made protein that recognises a specific target, for example a protein on the surface of tumour cells. Names end in "-mab".
Cancer of the plasma cells in the bone marrow, which make antibodies. It can affect the bones, kidneys and blood.
Treatment given before the main treatment, usually surgery, to shrink the tumour and see how it responds.
Abnormal, uncontrolled growth of cells. It can be benign or malignant. "Malignant neoplasm" means cancer.
Survival attributable to cancer, removing deaths from other causes. It is used to compare countries and periods.
A fall in neutrophils, white blood cells that fight infection. A common effect of chemotherapy. Fever with neutropenia is an emergency.
A gene that, when altered, pushes the cell to divide out of control. It works like a stuck accelerator.
The medical specialty that deals with cancer. It includes medical, radiation, surgical and paediatric oncology and haemato-oncology.
Care that relieves symptoms and suffering and supports the family at any stage of a serious illness. It is not limited to the last days.
The medical specialty that studies tissues and cells under the microscope. The pathologist's report confirms whether there is cancer and what type.
A protein some tumour cells use to put the brakes on lymphocytes. Measuring it helps decide on some immunotherapies.
The expected course of a disease. In cancer it depends on the type, stage, tumour biology, the person and the response to treatment.
Treatment that uses ionising radiation to destroy cancer cells in a specific area of the body.
The return of a cancer after a period in which it could not be detected. Also called recurrence.
A decrease in or disappearance of signs of cancer. Complete remission means no disease is detected with available tests.
Cancer arising in bone or soft tissues, such as muscle, fat or blood vessels. It is uncommon.
A programme offering a test to people without symptoms to find a cancer or precancerous change in time. Breast, bowel and cervical screening are the most common.
A review of the diagnosis or treatment by another specialist or centre. It is a patient's right and should not offend the team.
Describes a genetic change that appears in a cell during life, for example in a tumour. It is not inherited.
A description of how far a cancer has spread: its size, whether it affects lymph nodes and whether it has reached other organs. Usually given from 0 to IV.
An infusion of blood stem cells, the patient's own or from a donor, after intensive chemotherapy. Often called a bone marrow transplant.
A drug that acts on a specific change in tumour cells, such as a mutation or an excess protein. It usually requires a biomarker.
A system for describing the stage of many solid tumours: T is the size or extent of the tumour, N the lymph nodes affected and M metastases.
A mass of abnormal tissue. It can be benign or malignant. Not all tumours are cancers.
A substance measured in the blood that can be raised in some cancers, such as PSA or CEA. It almost never diagnoses cancer on its own.
A gene that slows cell division or repairs damage. When it is lost, the cell loses a brake. Examples: TP53, RB1, BRCA1.
